canberra.title: Fatal Yerrabi Ponds swan mauling prompts calls for better protections from uncontrolled, unleashed dogs
canberra.snippet: The horrific mauling of Yerrabi Ponds’ black swan family has outraged a community that’s had enough of unleashed dogs in the ...
canberra.content:
The Yerrabi Ponds black swan family in the minutes before two dogs attacked. Photo: Supplied.

The horrific mauling of Yerrabi Ponds’ black swan family has outraged a community that’s had enough of unleashed dogs in the area.

The two adult swans and their three cygnets were being admired by families at the Amaroo/Horse Park Drive end of the pond on Saturday (22 August), where they’re known to forage and nest.

A Bonner woman, who requested to remain anonymous, was showing her husband and toddler son the waterbirds when a man approached the area with two dogs.

One was on leash and another, a smaller dog, was free to roam.

The woman said one swan started honking in warning to protect its cygnets.

The man was trying to call the smaller dog back, and the woman and her family stepped back to protect their young son.

“I heard [the man] say ‘no’ louder and louder,” the Bonner woman said.

“It grabbed one of the swans, took it to the side in the grass and started mauling it.”

During the chaos, the leashed dog grabbed hold of one of the cygnets.

“[The man] was yelling at both of them, but they weren’t responding.”

It all happened within about 10 minutes, with the man then running from the scene with his two animals.

ACT Wildlife was called and arrived to take the swan and cygnet to an emergency vet.

They didn’t survive.

The Bonner woman said the remaining swans seemed to understand that two of their family members were gone.

“One of the parents and the two cygnets … were calling out,” she said.

“It wasn’t honking, it was this really sad noise.”

Black swans are monogamous and can mate for life. It’s also been documented that they can grieve.

The Bonner woman said she was too nervous to return to the area where the attack occurred, given that people often walk their dogs off-leash around the pond.

“What if my little one had run across to the swans and that’s when the dogs attacked?” she asked.

“I’m a bit scared now of going by myself.”

What remains of the Yerrabi Ponds black swan family following the dog attack. Photo: Supplied.

Animal advocate and Forde resident Jo McKinley is a frequent visitor to Yerrabi Ponds, often visiting the black swan family each day.

“Every time I walk the lake, there’s always people stopped, mesmerised by how gorgeous this particular family of swans were,” she said.

“This has left the community devastated.”

Black swans are a fully protected native species under the Native Conservation Act 2014 and the Animal Welfare Act 1992. It is a crime to harm, catch or interfere with them.

The Domestic Animals Act 2000 also outlines penalties for a dog causing serious injury to another animal, with a maximum penalty of 100 units (about $16,000) or one year’s imprisonment. Failure to report dog attacks within five days is also an offence.

Ms McKinley’s called for a full investigation – and potential prosecution – of the man with the dogs (if he can be identified).

She also wants the ACT Government to establish fully enclosed off-leash dog areas at Yerrabi Pond, clearer signage about on-leash requirements in the area, increased ranger presence or patrols at Yerrabi Pond, public signage discouraging bread-feeding of waterbirds, and a public update from the relevant government agency on the status of this case.

“I’ve always cared about and had concerns for the ACT’s wildlife … but this is, for me, a little bit personal because I got to know this family and I continue to visit the mother swan and cygnets,” Ms McKinley said.

“It’s the most heartbreaking thing to know this mother swan has been left with her two cygnets on the lake, and they’re on their own.”

It is not permitted to have dogs off-leash on the path around Yerrabi Pond, and dogs must be kept on-leash on all of Canberra’s footpaths (regardless of whether they’re in an off-leash area).

An ACT Government spokesperson confirmed there was an active investigation into the swans’ deaths.

“We recognise that the loss of local wildlife can be upsetting for community members. As this is an active investigation, we are unable to provide further details on the incident at this time,” they said.

Canberra has nine fenced dog parks – three of which are located in Gungahlin.

The spokesperson reminded dog owners that it was their responsibility to ensure their pets are properly trained, socialised and managed when in public places.

“[They] are also expected to manage their dogs so that they do not disturb or endanger other animals,” they said.

“Where wildlife is present, owners should take additional care and leash their dogs if there is any risk that effective control may be compromised.”

You can find out more information about the rules for dogs in Canberra’s public places through City Services.

canberra.title: Police seek witnesses after teens struck in alleged hit-and-run
canberra.snippet: Two teenagers were taken to hospital after they were struck by a car in an alleged hit-and-run last month in south Canberra. An ACT Polic...
canberra.content:
2 September 2026

2 September 2026

Police are calling for information about this car, a grey or silver early-model hatchback or SUV. Photo: ACT Policing.

Two teenagers were taken to hospital after they were struck by a car in an alleged hit-and-run last month in south Canberra.

An ACT Policing spokesperson said the teenagers were hit by a vehicle in Wentcher Place, Richardson, at around 8:25 pm on 18 August 2026.

Paramedics treated the two teens at the scene before they were taken to hospital for further assessment.

“The driver of the vehicle allegedly failed to stop and render assistance, and did not exchange details with the victims,” the police spokesperson said.

The spokesperson said the vehicle believed to be involved in the incident was described as a grey or silver early model hatchback or SUV.

“Police are urging anyone who witnessed the incident, or who has CCTV or dash-cam footage of the vehicle in the Richardson area around the time of the incident, to come forward,” the police spokesperson said.

If you have information that could assist police, contact Crime Stoppers ACT on 1800 333 000. Quote reference number 8475383.

canberra.title: Zoo murderer Jude Wijesinghe wins appeal, has jail sentence reduced
canberra.snippet: The brutal killer who murdered a young woman at Canberra’s zoo has won his appeal and had the jail sentence for his horrific crime ...
canberra.content:
2 September 2026

Jude Luckshan Wijesinghe admitted murdering his co-worker Tshewang Choden. Photo: Facebook.

The brutal killer who murdered a young woman at Canberra’s zoo has won his appeal and had the jail sentence for his horrific crime reduced by several years.

Jude Luckshan Wijesinghe stabbed his co-worker Tshewang Choden, a 29-year-old from Bhutan, 14 times in a kitchen area at the National Zoo & Aquarium on 18 December 2023.

They both worked as chefs in the kitchen at the zoo’s Jamala Wildlife Lodge for over a year before he killed her. It appeared he was infatuated with her, while she had made it clear to him she was not interested.

When his sentencing began in the ACT Supreme Court, Ms Choden’s family told him, “You have taken something very precious from us”.

“Her love held our family together,” her brothers said.

“Every day is a struggle. We are broken.”

Wijesinghe pleaded guilty to murder. Late last year, ACT Supreme Court Chief Justice Lucy McCallum sentenced him to 30 years behind bars, with a non-parole period of 20 years.

As he had remained in jail since the day of the murder, he would have been eligible for parole in December 2043 while his total sentence would have expired in December 2053.

But he launched an appeal against his sentence, which was heard by the ACT Court of Appeal’s Justices John White SC, Andrew Muller and Darryl Rangiah in July.

His barrister, Dr Kylie Weston-Scheuber, argued that although Chief Justice McCallum had found his mental illness meant his moral culpability was reduced, she failed to properly take this into account upon sentencing or in determining the crime’s objective seriousness.

On Wednesday (2 September), Justice White said the appeals court would allow the appeal and set aside his original sentence.

Wijesinghe was resentenced to a total of 26-and-a-half years’ jail with an 18-year non-parole period.

This means the now-32-year-old will be eligible for parole in December 2041, while his total sentence will end in June 2050.

The Court of Appeal will publish the reasons for its decision in the future.

canberra.title: Police hunt for driver after man dies following alleged hit and run in Bega
canberra.snippet: A 73-year-old man has died in hospital after a suspected hit-and-run on the NSW South Coast earlier this week. Police are now appealing f...
canberra.content:
NSW Police are appealing for information from the public. Photo: SCM Jeans.

A 73-year-old man has died in hospital after a suspected hit-and-run on the NSW South Coast earlier this week.

Police are now appealing for information as investigations continue into the tragic incident.

About 12:30 pm on Monday 31 August 2026, emergency services were called to Newtown Road, Bega, following reports a man had been struck by a vehicle.

NSW Ambulance paramedics treated the 73-year-old at the scene before he was taken to South East Regional Hospital in a serious condition.

Officers attached to South Coast Police District were told the man was allegedly involved in an altercation with the female driver of another vehicle.

The man allegedly got out of his car and was walking towards the other vehicle when it reversed into him.

The vehicle then left the scene.

On Tuesday afternoon (1 September), police were notified that the 73-year-old man had died in hospital.

Specialist police from the Crash Investigation Unit have started investigating the matter.

Police would like to speak to anyone who was in the Newtown Rd area between 12 pm and 12:30 pm on Monday 31 August 2026.

In particular, police are hoping to speak with the driver of a grey or light blue 1997-2002 model Subaru station wagon that was seen in the area prior to the incident.

The driver is described as a woman believed to be in her 20s.

As inquiries continue, police are urging anyone with information about the incident – or was in the area at the time with any relevant dashcam/mobile phone footage – to contact Bega Police Station or Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

Original Article published on About Regional.

canberra.title: Tuggeranong reigns supreme on grand final day, but Gungahlin women steal sweet revenge
canberra.snippet: As one of the biggest sporting clubs in Canberra, Tuggeranong Vikings has high expectations for any team wearing its jersey. On Saturday,...
canberra.content:
2 September 2026

Start the conversation

The Tuggeranong Vikings Men’s first-grade side are John I Dent Premiers 2026. Photo: ACT Rugby Union Facebook.

As one of the biggest sporting clubs in Canberra, Tuggeranong Vikings has high expectations for any team wearing its jersey.

On Saturday, that was on full display with the Vikings represented in all six grades in ACT Rugby Union grand finals.

In the end, they won three grades, including the John I Dent Cup, with a 27-23 victory over arch-rivals Royals to secure their first men’s top-grade title since 2018 to cap off a remarkably successful day for the Vikings Club.

Tuggeranong’s success on Saturday, though, will no doubt get under the skin of some who see the Vikings as being akin to Collingwood in the AFL or the Broncos in the NRL, with resources to be envied by their rivals.

Envy brings with it a certain amount of animosity.

There was a bit of that on the weekend from some rival supporters, who questioned whether the Vikings had an advantage because all finals were played at the club’s home ground, Viking Park.

The reality is that Tuggeranong, through their licensed clubs, has developed the best rugby union facility in Canberra outside GIO, which, quite frankly, leaves the remainder of the suburban grounds for dead.

Another reality check is that, without the Vikings, the Brumbies might not have become a team.

The Canberra Kookaburras were bankrolled by the Vikings in 1994, creating the platform for the establishment of the Brumbies in 1996. There have been numerous incarnations of the Kookaburras over the years underwritten by the Tuggeranong Club.

There was even animosity when the Kookaburras became the Canberra Vikings.

It may not be an entirely popular sentiment amongst some, but the Vikings have raised the standard of rugby in Canberra, with every club lifting every time they face Tuggeranong.

Gungahlin Eagles Women’s grand-final-winning team 2026. Photo: Jaye Grieshaber.

As a Gungahlin Eagles supporter, I can speak from experience about the delight in victories over Tuggeranong, with the Eagles women’s grand final win over the Vikings especially sweet.

The 33-17 victory secured the Eagles their first premiership in the Women’s Premier 15s, with the side winning 14 of 15 games from the regular season through to the grand final.

The 98-nil loss to Tuggeranong in the Eagles’ debut season in 2022 is now very much a distant memory.

australia.title: Fatal Sydney shooting could be another case of mistaken identity, police say
australia.snippet: A man shot dead in Merrylands West was not known to police, in a case with similarities to Tuesday’s killing in Campbelltown Get our brea...
australia.content:
New South Wales police are investigating the shooting death of a man in Sydney’s west as a potential case of mistaken identity, marking the second fatal shooting incident in as many days.

Emergency services responded to reports of a shooting at a home in Merrylands West at about 3.15pm on Wednesday, where a man believed to be in his 30s sustained a gunshot wound.

The victim, who was yet to be formally identified, was treated by paramedics but died at the scene.

Police said the property was a location known to police for organised crime, but said “the victim has no links that we’re aware of to organised crime”.

At a press conference, Supt Simon Glasser said it was unclear what the man who was shot was doing at the location or his connection to the residents.

“The person who we believe has been shot has no adverse holdings with police. People that are linked to this address are known to … organised crime,” he said.

“It’s very early on in the investigation, however, there is a possibility that the wrong person has been shot by these offenders.”

The alleged shooting marks the second incident of its kind this week.

On Tuesday, 23-year-old Marco Tapia was shot dead in his bed as his family slept at about 3.40am after multiple attackers were believed to have forced their way into a two-storey home in Glen Alpine, near Campbelltown, in south-west Sydney.

That case was being investigated as a case of mistaken identity, police said, because Tapia was not known to authorities and had nothing more than a traffic offence on his record.

His martial arts gym remembered him in a public tribute overnight.

“We lost a real one today,” they wrote, adding: “Rest easy Marco, one of us forever.”

The Alameddine network, a notorious crime family, and the Coconut Cartel, an emerging crime-for-hire network, have allegedly become embroiled in a feud, spilling into shootings across Sydney in recent months.

Acting Supt Gretchen Atkins of Campbelltown police said on Tuesday she was aware of online posts about the Glen Alpine case and said everything was under consideration.

The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said the incidents showed gangland violence was out of control.

“We need to be very clear about the threat on our streets and that is dangerous organised criminals … innocent people have been in the firing line way too often,” she said.

“Whether it is a young man, a student sleeping in his bed at night [or] a grandfather who’s kidnapped and murdered,” referring to the Sydney grandfather Chris Baghsarian, who was taken from his home on 13 February and later found dead.

She suggested the government was not doing enough to stop the shootings.

But the police minister, Yasmin Catley, criticised Sloane, whose electorate is in Sydney’s eastern suburbs, over her position on the state’s gun buyback scheme, launched after December’s Bondi massacre.

“The member for Vaucluse, we must remember, is also the same person that wants to squash [national gun buyback reform],” Catley said.

“She wants more guns on the street and wants to blame the police for not doing their job … I’m not tolerating that, I won’t have a bar of that.”

The person who we believe has been shot has no adverse holdings with police. People that are linked to this address are known to Sydney to organised crime.

It’s very early on in the investigation. However, there is a possibility that the wrong person has been shot by those offenders.

What we learned, Wednesday 2 September

That’s a wrap on our live coverage for the day.

Before we go, let’s recap what made the top headlines:

  • Consent education advocate Chanel Contos urged Australia to enforce a social media opt-in algorithm to help reduce the influence of the “manosphere” on both men and women during a speech at the national press club, a move backed by independent MP Allegra Spender.

  • Australia will step up its support to fight transnational drug trafficking flowing through the Pacific, with Anthony Albanese announcing a $600m package at the Pacific Islands Forum.

  • The government and Qantas also confirmed more flights would travel between Brisbane and Koror, as part of the Palau Paradise Express direct air service.

  • Five Australians have been confirmed safe in the devastating Nepal-Tibet floods, meaning the number of unaccounted-for citizens has been revised from 43 missing on Tuesday morning to 38. Australia will also provide $8m in humanitarian and disaster relief supplies for Nepal.

  • Telstra did not prioritise systems that caused a major nationwide network failure and lacked the technical expertise to properly maintain them, an independent investigation into the telco’s 8 July network failure found.

  • Australia’s economy expanded by 0.4% in the three months to June, marking an expected, if less marked, slowdown in annual growth from 2.5% to 2.1% as rising interest rates and the high cost of living take their toll.

  • Victorian police have travelled to New South Wales this week to interview four people as part of their investigations into the sexual assault allegations linked to the Sydney Swans.

  • The NSW police commissioner has responded to a video that emerged over the weekend that shows a police officer boasting about “punching” a protester in the head “when he was down”, saying he does not “condone” the language but he needs to “understand the context of it”.

‘A possibility the wrong person has been shot’: NSW police investigate fatal shooting as a case of mistaken identity

Police are investigating a potential case of mistaken identity after a man was shot dead in Sydney’s west.

Emergency services responded to reports of a shooting at a Merrylands West home at about 3.15pm, where a man sustained a gunshot wound.

At a press conference, Supt Simon Glasser said it is unclear what the male who was shot was doing at the location or what his involvement was. He said:

The person who we believe has been shot has no adverse holdings with police. People that are linked to this address are known to Sydney to organised crime.

The victim has no links that we’re aware of to organised crime.

It’s very early on in the investigation. However, there is a possibility that the wrong person has been shot by those offenders.

The alleged shooting marks the second incident of its kind in Sydney’s west being investigated as a case of mistaken identity this week.

Benita Kolovos

One Nation accuses Liberals of ‘hubris’ over comments on majority government

In another interesting exchange from the Victorian housing debate, Warren Pickering accused the Liberal party’s housing spokesperson, David Southwick, of displaying “hubris” when suggesting they would govern in a majority come November.

Southwick told the crowd that while Liberals weren’t taking “anything for granted” and “no seat is safe”, he looked forward to working with his “Liberal National colleagues” to deliver a majority government.

To which Pickering replied: “Hubris, mate.”

Benita Kolovos

One Nation suggests Latrobe Valley for nuclear plant

Continuing on our last post on the Victorian housing debate, while most of the conversation stayed on topic, the most fiery interaction involved a back and forth between parties on energy policy.

Sonya Kilkenny was asked about property taxes and said that, unlike states such as WA, New South Wales and Queensland, Victoria did not have the “luxury” of using resource royalties to prop up its finances.

One Nation’s Warren Pickering, however, said Victoria was the “most energy-abundant” state in the country and should utilise coal and gas.

Kilkenny responded:

We are transitioning to renewables because renewables will provide certainty to the grid. They will ensure lower energy prices and deliver the jobs of the future.

Kilkenny asked Pickering what community he would propose putting a nuclear reactor in. The One Nation state leader replied:

We’ll put the nuclear reactor where it makes viable sense to do so, where we’ve got existing power line infrastructure out at Loy Yang.

He received applause from the crowd, but it’s unlikely to be well received in the Latrobe Valley.

On Monday, Pickering was joined by Pauline Hanson in the region, where they announced the party would not allow Loy Yang A to close in 2035 as planned and would scrap Victoria’s 1983 ban on building nuclear power if it wins government in November.

Jordyn Beazley

NSW police commissioner defends decision to keep sniffer dogs at music festivals

The NSW police commissioner has defended the decision to continue using drug detection dogs at music festivals, despite the government expanding access to pill testing, saying “police have a really significant role in supply reduction”.

On Wednesday the NSW government announced pill testing would resume at music festivals from October, but there will be no change to the use of sniffer dogs at music festivals.

Drug detection dogs has been found to prompt risky drug taking. Police, security guards, bag searches and sniffer dogs at music festivals can lead to riskier drug use as people may “pre-load”, or take all of their substances at once, to avoid detection.

The police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, said of the decision to continue to use drug detection dogs:

Police have a really significant role in supply reduction... The way that we use drug detection dogs at festivals is designed to make sure that we are focusing on those who want to supply drugs.

But I make it clear, drugs remain illegal and harmful, and I want anyone thinking of using drugs at a festival to understand that there can be consequences to their health.

The Redfern Legal Centre has criticised the decision, pointing to a 2019 coroner recommendation that drug detection dogs be scrapped.

The centre’s police accountability lead, Rian Terrell, said:

Having police and drug dogs at festivals where pill testing is available will deter young people from getting their pills tested, undermining the harm reduction outcomes of the scheme.”

Testing will be more effective and save more lives without drug dogs present.

Benita Kolovos

Victorian Labor use housing debate to announce 10-day planning process for small developments

We’re inching closer to the Victorian state election, which means plenty of politicians are on the event circuit.

The Australian Property Developers Association hosted the first debate this afternoon on housing, with the planning minister, Sonya Kilkenny, Coalition housing spokesperson, David Southwick, One Nation Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, and Family First’s Alex van der End subbing in after the Greens pulled out of the event.

Kilkenny kicked things off by announcing an expansion of its 10-day planning permit process to include developments of up to four homes on a block. She told the crowd:

Four homes that comply with the townhouse code will be approved in 10 days, council will not be able to object to the planning application. This is just one step in the reforms that we are delivering to ensure that we’re increasing supply so that more young Victorians ... are able to find a home close to the jobs that they want in the places they want to live, whether that is out in our greenfields or in our inner Melbourne suburbs areas that we know have been locked up for so long.

Southwick focused on the Liberals’ earlier annoucement that it would scrap the government’s target of 70% of new homes into established suburbs and 30% into growth areas, saying “wherever the market says is appropriate to build, we will build”.

Both the Liberals and One Nation said they would reduce the land tax threshold from the current level of $500,000 back to the old level of $300,000. Pickering also said he’d “roll back” windfall tax and impose a “two out, one in policy” for all regulatory requirements. He went on:

It was just baffling to me to understand how many new regulatory changes were introduced to Australian standards year after year after year with no revision of previous standards. There is so much overlap, and it’s it’s causing perpetual waste.

However, when asked which two regulations related to the housing industry he’d remove by the moderator, Michael Rowland, he couldn’t name any.

Australia and Pacific nations agree to maritime security deal to combat organised crime

Australia and Pacific nations have entered a maritime security deal to tackle increasing transnational and organised crime, including illicit drug trafficking.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and Pacific leaders have agreed to Waqa Moana, a Pacific-led maritime security initiative, on Wednesday.

Under the deal, the prime minister has announced a $600m support package.

The AFP will additionally invest $49m in new counter-transnational and organised crime programs across the region, adding to the $140m the AFP has pledged to contribute over the next four years to support regional security objectives.

Albanese has also announced a department of defence investment of $312m over the next 10 years.

Albanese has welcomed the “growing capability of Pacific countries to work together to address shared security challenges”. He said:

The Pacific is our home and our family. That’s why it’s in Australia’s interests to work with our Pacific partners to combat organised crime.

For the good of every country in the region, including our own – we need to work together to stamp out the illicit drug trade.

NSW police investigate fatal shooting in Sydney’s west

New South Wales police have launched an investigation into a fatal shooting in Merrylands West in Sydney.

Emergency services were called to a home around 3.15pm after reports of a shooting.

A man believed to be in his 30s sustained a gunshot wound and was treated by paramedics but died at the scene. He is yet to be formally identified.

Three charged after suspected ketamine allegedly hidden in baby formula tin

Three people have been charged with drug offences after authorities allegedly found vacuum-sealed bags of suspected ketamine stored inside a tin of baby formula during a home search in Sydney’s south-west.

A man and woman, both aged 30, were arrested following the search where police also allegedly found another 3kg of suspected ketamine in foil packets in a suitcase and plastic container around the property.

Authorities said suspected MDMA tablets, about $30,000 cash, a replica firearm and other items suspected to be linked to drug trafficking were found.

The home search formed part of a wider federal investigation by the Australian Border Force (ABF) after officers allegedly detected ketamine and cocaine in a 26-year-old man’s luggage in July.

The Sydney couple have both been charged with five counts of drug offences each.

The 26-year-old man, from the Czech Republic, was charged with importing a commercial quantity of border-controlled drugs.

NSW police commissioner responds to footage of police officer boasting about punching Sydney anti-Herzog protester

Jordyn Beazley

The NSW police commissioner has responded to a video that emerged over the weekend that shows a police officer boasting about “punching” a protester in the head “when he was down”, saying he does not “condone” the language but he needs to “understand the context of it”.

The police body-worn camera footage, which was widely shared on social media over the weekend, revealed a male police officer telling his colleagues during the 9 February rally at Sydney town hall protesting against a visit by the Israeli president, Isaac Herzog: “I fucking pumped that cunt.”

A female officer can be heard replying, “So funny,” before the male officer says: “Then I punched him in the head when he was down.”

Guardian Australia understands the video relates to legal proceedings from a protester who was charged with assaulting police. They were one of three protesters who on Friday had the charges against them dropped.

The police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, was asked about the video on Wednesday during a press conference. He said:

The language is something that I don’t condone, but I need to understand the context of it. I think it’s appropriate that I leave that to the Lecc [Law Enforcement Conduct Commission] to actually conduct their investigations.

The police minister, Yasmin Catley, was also asked about the video during the same press confernce. She said:

I do not condone that language whatsoever. But what I would ask is, do we not all agree that we should have an independent investigation into this matter, and don’t we all agree that that should be at arm’s length of the government and the police? Yes, we absolutely should, because that’s the right thing to do, and that’s exactly what we’re doing.

The police watchdog, the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission, is investigating allegations of police brutality at the protest after it was referred for investigation by Greens MP, Sue Higginson.

Read the full story:

Police not expecting update on sexual assault investigation linked to Sydney Swans for eight weeks

Victorian police have travelled to New South Wales this week to interview four people as part of their investigations into the sexual assault allegations linked to the Sydney Swans.

Separate to the investigation, in August five Sydney Swans players were stood down for the rest of the season for breaching the club’s standards, including drinking and bringing women back to their hotel after their round 23 win over Essendon.

Police said they spoke to four men aged between 25 and 30 this week in Sydney’s eastern suburbs.

Police said they believe they have now identified all parties who were in the room at the time of the alleged incident and are not looking for anyone further.

The investigation remains ongoing. No one has been arrested or charged in relation to the allegations.

AFP raid Melbourne property in alleged corruption probe

Nino Bucci

The Australian federal police are searching properties in Melbourne on Wednesday as part of their investigation into alleged corruption within the building industry.

An AFP spokesperson confirmed in a statement that it had executed warrants in the Melbourne suburb of Keilor.

The search warrants are part of the AFP’s response to allegations of corruption in the Victorian building industry.

There is no threat to public safety.

Further comment will be made at an appropriate time.

Last month, the premier, Ben Carroll, announced a royal commission into “the nature and extent of corruption, criminal conduct and serious misconduct in relation to major construction projects in Victoria”.

Nick Visser

That’s all for me. Achol Arok will take it from here and guide you into the evening. Take care!

Luca Ittimani

First home loan applications hit three-month high, brokers’ company says

First home buyers’ loan applications hit a three-month high in August, Loan Market reports.

The mortgage brokers’ group has previously recorded falling loan applications from all groups over the months leading up to June, in the wake of interest rate rises and the budget’s cuts to investor tax breaks.

Investor loan applications fell back to their lowest numbers so far this year in August, after a slight pickup in July, Loan Market said. Separate Reserve Bank data earlier this week showed credit growth for property investors slowed sharply in July.

First home buyers’ applications bounced back from their decline and rose 6% from July to August, Loan Market reported. We reported on early signs of this recovery last week:

While separate data on other owner-occupier applications was not reported, pre-approvals for owner-occupier loans have dropped 12.6% in August 2026 compared to the same month last year, the group said. Investors’ pre-approvals have more than halved, down 55% in August 2026 from 2025.

Australia to provide $8m in humanitarian and disaster relief supplies for Nepal

The Australian government is providing $8m in humanitarian support to Nepal, including nearly 1,500 hygiene kits, hundreds of menstrual kits and 2,200 solar lights with phone chargers.

An air force aircraft carrying the humanitarian and disaster relief supplies was set to arrive in Nepal today.

The plane will also carry five large community lighting towers, 432 shelter tool kits that include shovels, saws and machetes, and nearly 900 tarpaulins and rope.

There are 18 Australian response team personnel in Nepal to support the crisis response, the government says.

Chalmers hails ‘resilient’ economy, but experts less impressed

Patrick Commins

Here’s what Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, had to say about this morning national accounts figures which showed economic growth was weak but better than expected in the June quarter:

This is a robust result in challenging international circumstances. It shows the resilience of Australia’s economy in the face of global uncertainty and conflict.

Annual growth in Australia was as strong or stronger than every major advanced economy – equal to the United States and much stronger than the rest.

While global circumstances are challenging and people are under pressure, we’ve got a lot going for us and we can see some of this reflected in today’s figures.

And here are a couple of (less positive) early impressions from economists: Stephen Smith, a partner at Deloitte Access Economics, said:

Today’s national accounts data confirm that the Australian economy is going sideways.

Without the spending on motor vehicles, household consumption growth would have been closer to just 0.1% in the quarter – far too weak to suggest households are shrugging off cost-of-living challenges.

Today’s accounts show too little growth and too much inflation.

Brendan Rynne, chief economist at KPMG, said:

The latest national accounts data … reveals an Australian that is at the crossroads.

Growth is stalling, it is cheaper to hire people than it is to invest in capital, productivity is continuing to go backwards, wages are falling in real terms and the ‘free gift’ that improving terms of trade offers has reversed.

These results continue to raise the bigger policy picture of what needs to happen differently to turn around Australia’s declining standard of living.

The outlook can best be summarised as continuing to muddle along.

Albanese says the government retains hope for positive news out of Nepal, but it’s a ‘very difficult time’ for many

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is speaking in Palau, where he is visiting for the Pacific Islands Forum. He said today’s news that another five Australians had been confirmed safe in Nepal after the floods was good news, but the government still holds grave fears for the 38 other missing citizens.

We hope, of course, for positive news … and we’re doing everything we can to work with authorities. We think of all of the families at this very difficult time. And also for the very broader Nepalese–Australian community that is a large and growing larger community as well.

This is a very difficult time.

Tom McIlroy

Social media ‘one of society’s biggest challenges’: Chalmers

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, says social media algorithms are one of the biggest challenges facing society today, hitting out at the business model of big platforms seeking to polarise users.

Sexual consent campaigner Chantel Contos spoke today at the National Press Club in Canberra and Chalmers was asked about her push for platforms to be required to offer opt-in functions for algorithms.

“From a personal point of view, if you made a short list of the biggest problems that we’ve got in our society, I think the role of social media would be on that list,” he said.

Chalmers said content on big platforms is too often divisive and violent.

What President Obama said not that long ago, which is social media has become about affirmation rather than information … I think that’s a really neat way of describing what we’re up against as a country.

It is a huge challenge, and our society, our social cohesion, the way that we come at big problems, including in my part of the shop, in the economy, is hampered, not helped, by the way that algorithms are dominating people’s day.

australia.title: Ray Hadley used homophobic slur against Alan Jones and said he wanted to bury him ‘figuratively and literally’, court hears
australia.snippet: Hadley is giving evidence in trial of former 2GB rival Jones, 85, who has pleaded not guilty to 22 indecent assault and sexual touching c...
australia.content:
Broadcaster Ray Hadley has told a Sydney court he used a homophobic slur and derogatory names when talking about his colleague Alan Jones, after 2GB withdrew a secret offer of a $4m contract to take over Jones’s coveted breakfast slot.

In one text message read out in court, Hadley said he won’t rest until he buries Jones, “figuratively and literally” and he will “tear his supporters apart”.

In another text, on the eve of the Sydney Morning Herald publishing an investigation into allegations against Jones in late 2023, Hadley wrote: “That cunt will be in the foetal position when he reads the story in the morning. It’s been 50 years in the making.”

Hadley agreed during cross-examination by defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC that he had a “tumultuous relationship” with Jones.

Jones is on trial over 20 charges of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching involving six men. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty.

On his second day giving evidence at Downing Centre local court, Hadley testified that a colleague had told him Jones had “marshalled the troops and said ‘Dig up some dirt on Hadley’”.

Hadley in 2019 had walked into Jones’s office after being accused of an unrelated assault against a colleague, and called the breakfast host “a cunt and a dog”, according to a police statement from the time that was raised in court.

The assault allegation against Hadley was dropped when 2GB CCTV showed nothing had happened, Hadley told Jones’s trial.

Hadley agreed that he had “an animosity towards [Jones] at that time”. He said he often called him a “grub”, and that in a text exchange shown to him by Bashir he had called Jones “a faggot”.

Bashir, when defending Jones in court, has said the allegations against her client were “trial by media” fuelled by hatred and jealousy. Hadley “wanted to destroy” Jones and to “tear him apart”, the barrister has said previously.

Bashir put to Hadley on Wednesday that he was having a difficult time after his secret contract to replace Jones was torn up and Jones was re-signed in May 2019 for two more years.

“Not at all, I maintained the same job I’d done for the previous 17 years and inadvertently Mr Jones had doubled my salary,” Hadley replied.

Hadley disagreed that the pinnacle of his career was attaining the breakfast radio slot, insisting that “going from $2m to $4m” while remaining on the Ray Hadley Morning Show was the pinnacle.

Hadley told the court he was approached by management in late 2018 and they said they had had enough of Jones and his then-defamation cases and offered him the job.

“I didn’t want to get out of bed at 1.30am, but the money made me do it,” Hadley said.

Bashir suggested to Hadley that a later text to Jones – who was suffering from ill health – was “rubbish” because Hadley said “I love you”.

Hadley explained that when he said “I love you” he added “above ground” because Jones had said if he hadn’t got the flu shot the illness may have killed him and he “would be in Rookwood [cemetery]”.

Late in the afternoon Hadley admitted he had winked at someone in the public gallery, because he mistakenly believed she was the Herald reporter who had written that he looked “scruffy” on Tuesday.

The Herald actually referred to Hadley as speaking “gruffly”.

Judge Glenn Walsh ordered the sheriff to investigate whether an unidentified journalist had contacted Hadley while he was giving his evidence as it would constitute a direct violation of his directions not to speak to anyone about his evidence.

The trial continues with Hadley in the witness box on Thursday.

australia.title: Afternoon Update: Global heating forecast to hit at least 1.8C, DNA tests to help identify Nepal flood victims, and shark drones
australia.snippet: Want to get this in your inbox every weekday? Sign up for the Afternoon Update here , and start your day with our Morning Mail newsletter...
australia.content:
Good afternoon.

Global heating will reach at least 1.8C under even the most optimistic future, well beyond the Paris agreement goal of 1.5C, according to a UN report that warns every fraction of temperature rise intensifies destructive extreme weather, ecosystem loss, and island and coastal city submersion.

The report by the Nairobi-based UN Environment Programme said “there are no good outcomes above 1.5C”. Human health, water supplies, nature, cities, infrastructure and economies could all be severely damaged. Some losses would be irreversible and many communities may have to relocate.

But scientists say the world could get back to 1.5C through deep, rapid emissions cuts and removing carbon from the atmosphere through steps such as establishing vast new forests alongside, not as an alternative to, deep cuts in fossil fuel pollution.

Top news

  • Jury in Bruce Lehrmann’s Queensland rape trial may face questions about prior knowledge of case

  • Off-grid UK-Australian couple given more access to children who were removed from home in Italy

  • Ray Hadley used homophobic slur against Alan Jones after 2GB withdrew offer of $4m breakfast radio gig, court hears

  • USS Abraham Lincoln arrives at Thai port after gruelling 270 days at sea

  • More than a third of prenatal reports to NSW protective services not investigated, ombudsman finds

In video

At the Nepal Police hospital in Kathmandu, grieving families are lining up to provide DNA samples in the hope of identifying victims of the devastating floods. Guardian Australia’s Cait Kelly, on the ground in Nepal, has documented the harrowing accounts of those searching for missing loved ones, including survivors who lost their parents.

You can watch the video here, and read Kelly’s feature story here.

What they said …

“If you made a short list of the biggest problems that we’ve got in our society, I think the role of social media would be on that list.” – Jim Chalmers

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, says social media algorithms are one of the biggest challenges facing society today, hitting out at the business model of big platforms seeking to polarise users.

Chalmers added “our society, our social cohesion, the way that we come at big problems, including in my part of the shop, in the economy, is hampered, not helped, by the way that algorithms are dominating people’s day”.

Podcast

Tupac’s murder: solved at last?

Thirty years after Tupac Shakur’s death, a man has been found guilty of killing the hip-hop legend.

William Shaw speaks to the Guardian about the star’s life, legacy and untimely death.

Listen to the episode here.

Before bed read

Before a shark attacked Sydney teacher and mother Leah Stewart in June, drone surveillance was not permitted at Coogee beach because it lies directly under the flight path from Sydney airport’s east-west runway. But under a $34m initiative by the state government that out in July, 38 of Sydney’s ocean beaches, including Coogee, now receive dawn-to-dusk drone monitoring year round.

So what’s involved in flying a shark drone? Penry Buckley joined a morning of shark surveillance to find out.

australia.title: Queensland police investigate after 5,500 sheep worth $1.7m stolen from farm
australia.snippet: Police say the sheep were stolen from a property 830km west of Brisbane between February and May Get our breaking news email , free app o...
australia.content:
Queensland police are investigating after about 5,500 Dorper sheep worth more than $1.7m were allegedly stolen from a western Queensland farm.

Police said the sheep were stolen from a property outside Blackall, about 830km west of Brisbane, between February and May this year.

Detective Sen Sgt Paul Elliot, from the rural and stock crime squad, said the sheep had an estimated value of about $1.7m (£899,000).

They are fitted with white National Livestock Identification System tags and are Dorper sheep, a breed with white wool but a black face. Both ewes and rams were taken.

Elliot urged anyone with information about the theft or who had seen Dorper sheep matching the description in the area to come forward.

“Livestock theft investigations can be complex, often spanning large geographical areas, which is why we work closely with producers, saleyards, transport operators and industry stakeholders to identify offenders and disrupt criminal activity,” he said.

The AgForce general president, Shane McCarthy, said it was a “a concerning amount of sheep that have been stolen” and would have a significant effect on the farm’s bottom line.

“We’re seeing a concerning rise in the number of incidents like this happening across the state,” he said. “We would trust that the police are taking these matters very, very seriously.”

He said a sheep theft of that scale would require a plan, time and more than one person. Sheep rustlers will sometimes take a group into a property where they can be bred to gain the value of their progeny and then slowly sold to abattoirs over time.

Thefts are often discovered at the abattoir, he said.

“I would say that it’s been thought out for a while,” he said. “I would suggest that one or two sheep here and there, even up to you know 10 or so sheep, is opportunistic. When we’re talking these numbers, they’re organised.”

It is not yet clear how the sheep were stolen, such as being loaded on to several trucks or mustered.

Dorpers are bred to be eaten, not for wool.

The Blackall-Tambo mayor, Andrew Martin, said the herd was probably not all taken in one night.

“I’m suspecting a number of smaller hits and sneaking them off to the abattoir or whatever it is they’re doing with them,” he said.

Farms in some parts of Queensland can rival the size of some countries. Stock theft is typically discovered during a muster.

Martin, who has farmed Dorper sheep, said some properties have as many as 25,000 sheep. It is possible to lose thousands by them escaping, from an animal attack or just miscounting them, without noticing for a long period of time, he said.

“This is an age-old problem. Poddy dodging is a bit of an art, and it’s been going on ever since poddies were there to be dodged,” he said, using Australian slang for stock theft.

world.title: Guinea-Bissau voters approve new constitution expanding presidential powers
world.snippet: Changes include fewer seats in parliament and new rules on presidential candidates ahead of December elections Guinea-Bissau voters have ...
world.content:
Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution significantly expanding presidential powers ahead of elections due in December.

According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago.

The turnout for Sunday’s referendum was reportedly over 55%, amounting to an estimated 544,060 people.

The new constitution will reduce the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cut electoral constituencies from 29 to 12. New provisions will require presidential candidates to have lived continuously in the country for at least five years before the vote, which is believed to target diaspora-based politicians with significant followings.

The referendum’s outcome is expected to pave the way for December’s elections, which many hope will steady the political landscape in Guinea-Bissau, which has been through a series of politically turbulent periods since its declaration of independence from Portugal was globally recognised in 1974. Since then it has had at least 10 coup attempts, half of which have been successful.

The most recent came after last November’s disputed presidential elections. Both candidates declared themselves winners, citing electoral malpractice by the other’s camp. The military forcefully intervened, setting up a transitional ruling council headed by Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, a former military chief of general staff.

Na Man said: “What we want after this referendum is to allow whoever wins the elections to see out their mandate without hindrance.”

Nelson Moreira, the second vice-president of the transitional council, said the outgoing constitution, which came into effect in 1993, had often been cited as “the cause of instability in Guinea”.

The leading opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), which was barred from fielding a presidential candidate in the 2025 election, had asked its supporters to boycott the referendum, which it called a democratic farce.

“What will happen on 30 August is the continuation of the coup d’état carried out on 26 November,” its leader, Domingos Simões Pereira, had said.

world.title: Almost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts find
world.snippet: Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities Almost half of t...
world.content:
Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.

Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.

Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa.

The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.

The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.

Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.

The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.

The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.

Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”

The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.

Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”

Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.

Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers.

Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.

Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.

“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.

Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.

world.title: South African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clash
world.snippet: Cape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risks Airlink insists flyby conducted according to regulations A pre-game stunt involving...
world.content:
A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks. The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by the local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Test between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.

The flight tracking service Flightradar24 estimated that the lead jet passed just 41-46 feet (12-14 metres) above the roof of Cape Town Stadium, with the crowd and the world’s top-ranked rugby teams below. The second jet, which was very close behind, flew through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.

Airlink, a sponsor of the South Africa rugby union team, said the flyby was conducted according to safety regulations. The airline said that it was carefully planned and rehearsed, with the aircraft flying at 150 knots (172 mph), when they went over the stadium. Each jet had three senior captains on board, Airlink said, operating in the roles of a commander, a co-pilot and a safety officer. The jets were not carrying any passengers.

“Airlink notes the concerns expressed in various social media and online forums regarding yesterday’s formation flyby over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium,” Airlink said on Sunday. “The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude, at around 150 knots. The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby.”

South African rugby union has a tradition of stadium flybys at big games, starting when a Boeing 747 flew over a stadium in Johannesburg before the 1995 World Cup final between the same teams, who are fierce rivals. But the flyby last weekend was especially low and dramatic, generating global interest after it was shown as part of the pre-game broadcast, and sparking a flurry of videos shot by witnesses.

Some aviation experts questioned whether the margin for error was too small. “Basically, that lead aircraft … was kind of like dodging over the roof and climbing over the one side and dipping below and then climbing over the other side. That was a little bit uncomfortable,” Chris Martinus, president of Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association South Africa, said. “[If] something adverse happens, you just don’t have options at that kind of altitude.”

Keith Tonkin, an Australian aviation consultant and former military and commercial pilot, said yesteron Monday that the Embraer passenger jets – which are small-to-medium jets designed for regional flights – were not designed or intended for that kind of low-level operation and warned against the precedent.

“The bigger picture is that a benchmark has been established and others may expect to do something similar, and that’s not going to end well,” Tonkin said. He added that turbulence or a bird strike at such a low altitude could leave the pilots with too little room to manoeuvre without hitting the stadium.Airlink said flight data recorded by both aircraft confirmed their flights were performed within civil aviation safety limits for speed and altitude.

world.title: Countries legally obliged to consider slavery reparations, says UN committee
world.snippet: Guidance says states must implement ‘comprehensive measures’ to address legacy of racial discrimination A UN committee has said countries...
world.content:
A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.

Guidance published on Monday by the committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD) said the obligations arose from ⁠a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place.

The committee described the approach as a “paradigm ⁠shift” away from debates over historical responsibility that have often been used by governments to resist reparations ​claims.

“States parties must implement comprehensive reparatory measures for ‌people of African descent, ‌covering all aspects of remedies,” said the UN document, which may be cited in courtrooms.

At least 12.5 ‌million Africans were taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries in what CERD called the largest forced displacement in history.

Calls for reparations – ranging from official apologies to financial compensation – have gained momentum internationally, though opponents argue states and institutions should not be held responsible for historical crimes. The EU and Britain abstained from a UN resolution ‌on slavery in March.

Some states have sought to dodge claims for justice in courtrooms by arguing that there were no international laws outlawing the slave trade ​at the time – the so-called intertemporality principle.

But the UN document argues that, regardless of whether slavery and the slave trade were illegal under the laws of the day, countries remain responsible under current international obligations to tackle their continuing effects.

“Irrespective of the legal characterisation of the original historical acts, states parties remain bound ⁠by their present obligations under the convention to address structural inequalities,” the UN document ​says.

Financial compensation alone is ​not sufficient, it adds, urging “transformative” measures including ​opening archives, revising public memorials and establishing independent truth commissions.

Pela Boker Wilson, a committee expert ​from Liberia who helped draft ‌the document, said ​she expected states ​to move beyond broad expressions of regret and review policies and laws.

“We are calling on state parties to take concrete and meaningful action,” she told Reuters. “We want to affirm the dignity of those whose suffering was denied, whose suffering was minimised or forgotten.”

world.title: Morocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PM
world.snippet: Pedro Sánchez says two countries cooperating and accuses Israel and Russia of spreading fake news about migration Spain’s prime minister,...
world.content:
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has said there is no evidence to suggest the Moroccan government was behind last month’s massive border crossing into Ceuta but accused Israel and Russia of spreading disinformation.

As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter the Spanish enclave at the end of July. The influx of about 70,000 men, women and children unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.

Despite speculation that Rabat may have engineered the mass crossing as a means of showing its displeasure at Spain’s rapprochement with Algeria, Sánchez said there was nothing to indicate the involvement of the Moroccan authorities.

“There’s no information from any intelligence agency that raises doubts over the involvement of Moroccan authorities,” he told Cadena Ser radio on Monday. “Cooperation with Morocco is frankly positive. I’d like to stress that we need to be aware that this crisis can be resolved only through cooperation – and not through a lack of trust in Morocco, which would only further aggravate the already complex situation we have in Ceuta.”

Sánchez said fake news had been pumped out on social media accounts “associated with Russia, Israel and the international far right that always use migration to attack not just Spain but also Europe”.

The accusation drew a furious response from Israel. The country’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, called it a “brazen lie”, adding: “Continuing to spread defamatory lies will not distract from Sánchez’s disgraceful failure to manage his country’s affairs.”

The ⁠Kremlin rejected allegations ⁠that ​Russia was connected to ⁠the Ceuta migration crisis, the ⁠RBC daily ​reported ‌on ‌Monday.

Sánchez repeated his assertion that the influx was due to the activities of “criminal gangs” who had used disinformation to falsely claim that a ruling by Spain’s supreme court meant that no one who entered Ceuta by swimming could be deported back to Morocco.

Although the overwhelming majority of the migrants crossed back into Morocco weeks ago, at least 5,000 people, including 1,200 minors, are still on the streets of Ceuta. Their continuing presence has led to clashes between some Ceuta residents and police, while some of the migrants have had their belongings burned while sleeping rough on beaches. On Saturday, four Moroccan migrants were arrested for throwing stones at Spanish soldiers.

Sánchez said there would soon be “sufficient capacity” to accommodate all those still in the enclave.

Spain’s conservative People’s party has accused the government of failing to protect the people of Ceuta. “It did nothing to avoid the invasion on 30 July and it’s doing nothing to stop the public order crisis that’s getting worse every day,” the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said last week.

Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, has described events in Ceuta as “an invasion and an act of war promoted by Morocco and allowed by Sánchez, who is incapable of responding because he is subservient to Morocco”.
